TWO MEN KILLED IN MOONSHINE RAID
Oklahoma City, Aug. 28.—Home Adrean, deputy sheriff, Stanley F. Weiss, federal prohibition officer, and Charlie Chandler, a negro moonshiner was killed and Claud Tyler, another deputy sheriff was seriously wounded today near Arcadia. 20 miles northeast of here, when the officers attempted to raid a still.

A posso left here for the scene of the shooting. Armed negroes guarded the approach to the still.
charles-chandler-arcadia-1920-08-28.A2:
FORM NEGRO MOB
Race War May Start Over Raid on Still.

Three Dead and One Seriously Wounded in Battle.
Oklahoma City, Okla., Aug. 28.—Three persons, including a negro, were killed and another was seriously wounded in a pitched gun battle at Arcadia, Okla., 18 miles northeast of this city early today.

The dead: Deputy Sheriff Homer Adrean, Prohibition Enforcement Officer Stanley Weiss and Charles Chandler, negro.

Seriously wounded: Deputy Sheriff Claude Tyler.

The shooting affair, according to reports reaching here, followed an attempt of the officers to raid the home of Chandler, who is alleged to have been operating a still. The negro began firing when the officers surrounded his premises.

Adrean and Weiss were instantly killed. Tyler was shot in the neck. It is believed Tyler killed the negro as he lay wounded. One hundred negrces were said to be organizing near the scene of the tragedy.

Fear of mob violence was expressed by local police. Hundreds of armed possemen left here for Arcadia immediately after the news reached the city.

Homer Adrean, deputy sheriff of Oklahoma county, and S. E. Weiss, federal enforcement officer, of Oklahoma City, are dead: Claude Tyler, deputy sheriff of Oklahoma county, lies seriously wounded, with balls in neck and shoulder: Charles Miller, negro, is dead and his 18-year old son, Austin, is slightly wounded and in jail, as the result of a pre-arranged raid on a still operated by Charles Chandler, on the W. T. Walker farm, near Meridian, at 7:30 o'clock Saturday morning. Reed Miller, another enforcement officer, was reported missing at first, but he turned up later with Chandler's son in tow. At 10 o'clock last night the enforcement officers, Stanley Weiss and Reed Miller, received instructions from County Attorney Cargill, Oklahoma City, that a still was being operated on the Walker farm, five miles south and two miles west of Meridian, and one mile south of the Empire test well.

They were instructed to "crush it."

Calling on the sheriff's office for aid, Homer Adrean and Claude Tyler, deputies, were detailed to accompany the sleuths.

The officers reached the "corn mill" at 11 o'clock Friday night and lay in wait until after 7 o'clock this morning, when Chas. Chandler, aged 54, the father of 12 children, and his son, Austin, aged 18, appeared.
The two colored men were captured without a struggle and marched to the Chandler home at the top of the hill.

Deputy Tyler accompanied Chandler into the house, for the purpose of locating stored booze.

Adrean and Weiss remained on guard outside the door.

Miller was left to guard the still a hundred yards away.

Austin Chandler was in charge of Adrean outside the house.

At this point all stories regarding the killing conflict.

The generally accepted one is that Chandler accompanied Tyler upstairs, and while the officer was searching for booze the negro grabbed Tyler's automatic and began firing at him. Tyler was shot twice in the

How Homer Adrian, Stanley Weiss, and Charlie Chandler, alleged moonshiner, was killed, and himself wounded in the raid was told by Claudie Tyler in a doctor's office, at Edmond 10 miles south of Arcadia, where he had been taken to have his wounds dressed. According to Tyler's story, the three officers and Reed Miller, prohibition enforcement agent, succeeded in entering the house in which the still was believed to be located, without resistance.
Chandler was found in the house and immediately arrested. Miller took up his position as guard on the outside of the house, while Tyler, leaving Chandler in the custody of Adrian and Weiss, went upstairs to search for the alleged still. At the time of Chandler's arrest there apparently was no one else on the lower floor, Tyler says that while searching a room at the head of the stairs he heard a slight noise at his rear, and turning, faced Chandler with an automatic pistol levelled at him. He grappled with the negro, and in the melee that followed, was shot through the shoulder and suffered a scalp wound.
He fell to the floor stunned, while Chandler rushed the stairs. A number of pistol shots followed, Tyler says, and when he recovered sufficiently to make the stairs he found Adrian, Weiss and Chandler all dead on the floor, shot through the head. Miller, who was on the outside, rushed toward the house at the sound of the first shot and just before entering, encountered another negro coming out, shot through the arm. He was placed under arrest and handcuffed to a post. Tyler believes the second negro is a son of Chandler, and was in hiding at the time of his father's arrest.
Investigation by Tyler and Miller of the roof in which the shootings occurred revealed a second pistol. said not to have been used by either of the officers or the dead negro. Tyler expressed the opinion that the second negro freed Chandler in some way.

**Race Trouble Imminent**

Six motor cars containing negroes, heavily armed, were reported to have left Edmund, a town about 15 miles north of here, and three automobiles also containing negroes are reported to have left Arcadia about 23 miles northeast of here, for Oklahoma City, according to messages received here today at the office of County Attorney Cargill. It was said at the county attorney's office that Cargill was arming his deputies in anticipation of any eventuality that might arise should the negroes be bound here for a clash with officers.

**Story of The Crime**

Claude Chandler, son of Charles Chandler, negro, who was killed near Arcadia, 23 miles northeast of here, when federal and county officers attempted to raid a "moonshine" still, it is believed fired the shots which killed two of the officers.

O. A. Cargill county attorney, believes the boy killed Homer Adrean, deputy sheriff, and Stanton E. Weiss, federal prohibition enforcement officer.

G. E. Johnson, sheriff, agrees with Cargill's theory that the boy killed Weiss, but believes Adrean was killed by the elder Chandler, the alleged "moonshiner" and bootlegger who was killed in the battle. He bases his theory on the position of the three bodies after the shooting. Weiss' body was found near the back of the house he said, while Adrean's and Chandler's bodies were found on the same side of the Chandler house, several yards apart. He believes Adrean and Chandler killed each other, but did not know which of the two men had fired first.

Two Negroes Lynched For Striking Down Guard Attorney Later Declares One Innocent of Attack Made in Quitting Chain Gang
CORINTH, Miss., Aug. 28.—Blutcher Higgins and Dan Calicut, negroes, who surrendered yesterday after escaping from the county chain gang, were hanged to-day to a telegraph pole just outside the jail after a mob had forced the jailer to turn over his keys.

In making their escape, it was alleged, Higgins and Calicut struck down and severely injured one of the guards. Two other prisoners escaped at the same time, but one of these was recaptured.

County Attorney Johnston declared that "at least one" of the negroes lynched was innocent of any part in the attack on the guard.
dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A3:
TWO NEGROES FALL IN LYNCHING PARTY Escape From Convict Guard After Hitting Him on Head, Returned; Lynched Later
(Associated Press)

CORINTH, MISS., Aug. 28—Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicent, negroes were lynched here early today by a mob numbering between 75 and 100 men after J. D. King, jailer, had been forced at the point of a gun to give up the keys to the jail. Immediately after hanging the negroes to a telegraph pole near the jail the mob dispersed quietly and no further disorder took place.

The negroes lynched are said to have escaped from a chain gang with two others yesterday after James Whitehurst, a guard, was knocked on the head. They returned and surrendered to the sheriff. A third was captured near here late today. Whitehurst is expected to recover.

A coroner's inquest into the lynching was begun today and will be continued Monday. Thomas H. Johnston, county prosecuting attorney, declared "at least one" of the negroes lynched was innocent of any part in the felling of Whitehurst.
dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A11:
WHERE LYNCHING IS WINKED AT.
Only what can be expected to happen when mob rule undertakes to override law and administer justice is just what occurred at Corinth, Miss., where two Negroes were lynched following which the county attorney declares that "at least one" of the Negroes was innocent. No consideration, however, was given to any such possibility. No effort was made to determine whether the men so ruthlessly murdered were guilty or not guilty of any offense. It was apparently a case where any offense on the part of a colored man was sufficient to incense the mob and under such circumstances any Negro was likely to be deprived of his life.

No crime justifying the death penalty had been committed. It was a case where members of a county chain gang had in making their escapes struck down and severely injured one of the guards. It is not to be inferred that those men should not have been sought and punished for the assault, and if the condition of the injured man justified they should have had the charge against them deferred until the full extent of the injuries could be determined. Capital punishment was certainly not called for, and if it had been justice to a human being demands that he should have received it in accordance with the provisions of the law and at the hands of properly constituted authorities. The hot headed mob was unwilling to accord this justice. So eager were the murderers to take life that they didn't take the trouble to find out whether the Negroes who were taken out of jail after
dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A12:
CORINTH MOB IS CONDEMNED BY ALCORN CITIZENS Guard Declares Two Negroes Hanged Were Not Ones Who Assaulted Him--Guilty One Is Still at Large.
CORINTH, Miss., Aug. 30. (Spl.)—At a mass meeting held Sunday night at the First Baptist church here, in which the best citizens of the city and county attended, resolutions were passed condemning the mob which held a pistol on Jailer J. D. King Friday morning, forced him to turn over Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicut, negroes, and then hanged the blacks to a telegraph pole.

The coroner's jury will meet this afternoon. Hundreds of citizens, known not to have participated in the lynching, have been summoned and will be examined for service on the jury. The sessions probably will last several days, and it is expected arrests will be made.

James Whitehurst, the guard who was assaulted by one of the four negro prisoners who escaped from the jail, has declared that neither of the negroes who were hanged were implicated in the assault upon him. He says George York, the negro who struck him down and made the jail delivery possible, is still at large.

Citizens here are condemning the mob for hanging two innocent negroes.
dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A14:
B. G. Whitehurst, of Memphis, son of J. W. Whitehurst, guard at the jail 1.1 Corinth, Miss., who was brutally assaulted by two negro prisoners Wednesday, stated that the report that the two negroes hanged by a mob for the assault were not implicated and that the mob had hanged two innocent blacks, was an error.

Mr. Whitehurst said that he went to Corinth immediately after he heard of his father's injuries. His father, he said, told him that Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicutt, the two negroes who were lynched, were the ones who assaulted him. He said Callicutt called to him to attract his attention, and that Blutcher Higgins struck him with a shovel as he turned toward Callicutt. George York, a third negro who escaped and has not yet been apprehended, was standing near by with an ax in his hand.

The three negroes escaped, but Callicutt and Higgins returned to prison later and were lynched by the mob.

A coroner's jury is now investigating the lynching, according to reports from Corinth.
dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A17:
NEGROES LYNCHED BY MOB AT CORINTH ASSAULTING OF CHAIN GANG GUARD WHITEHURST WAS THE CAUSE. TWO MEN TAKEN FROM JAIL At Least One Was Innocent, Declares Prosecuting Attorney-Third Negro Captured After Lynching Now in Jail.
Corinth, Miss.—Aroused over the beating of Guard James Whitehurst by escaping negro convicts, a mob estimated at 100 persons assembled on a country road August 29 at midnight, came into town and stormed the Alcorn county jail and, after removing two of the negroes, hanged them to a telephone pole at the crossing of the Illinois Central and Southern railroads. As day dawned early risers received the first intimation of the double killing when they saw the bodies of the two negroes dangling in the air.

The third negro was recaptured and placed in jail here.

The mob gathered quietly, marched into town intent on a fixed purpose and grimly set about its task. Arriving at the county jail, J. D. King, jailer, was called to the door.

"Give us the keys to the cells," demanded one, backing up his words with a revolver, which he threw into the face of the custodian. Realizing that to oppose the crowd would be futile, King complied.

The mob took Blutcher Higgins and Dan Callicutt, two of the escaping negroes, who had voluntarily returned and surrendered themselves, and proceeded quietly to its work. The negros were taken to the crossing of the railroads on the outskirts of town, quickly strung up and the mob dispersed.

Immediately after the departure of the mob with their victims the jailer telephoned Sheriff Gray, who in turn telephoned County Attorney Johnston. The two officials made a hurried investigation and, after getting all the information Mr. King had, started out to find the mob. But the leaders had directed the mob so well and the lynchings had been performed with so little commotion that the officials were unable to find any trace of them. No intimation of the fate of the negroes was had until their bodies were discovered.

A coroner's jury, after hearing the testimony of Sheriff Gray and inmates of the jail, adjourned the hearing. Prosecuting Attorney Thomas H. Johnston assisted in the examination of the witnesses.

"If I can get any information on which to base it there will be the most vigorous prosecution in this case the county has ever seen," Mr. Johnston, He characterized the incident as the most disgraceful in the history of the county.

"This mob has made a fearful mistake," he said, "and beyond question has killed at least one innocent negro. You can say," he concluded vehemently, "there will be a determined investigation and some one will have to answer for this fearful smirch upon the name of Alcorn county and this blow to justice and right and the law."

Guard Whitehurst, who was knocked in the head by negroes he was working on the chain gang, has improved greatly and it was declared that his recovery is certain.

dan-calicut-corinth-1920-08-27.A27:
CORINTH'S SHAME
CORINTH, Mississippi, reports the "orderly lynching" of two Negroes Friday night. A member of the chain gang in an attempt to escape assaulted the guard, knocking him unconscious injuring him rather severely though not fatally. Two were arrested and one made his escape. The lynching was "orderly" because apparently there was no resistance. A Corinth dispatch rays the mob "demanded" the keys of the jailer, took the prisoners, left the jail in a "quiet manner" and murdered their victims on a county road.

Now, the injured guard says at least one of the murdered colored men was innocent, because one of the men lynched was in front of him while the assault was committed from behind. He thinks the man who committed the assault was the man who got away in which case both of the murdered prisoners were innocent, and even the one who escaped was not guilty of a crime that merited death at the hands of the law.

The best citizens of the town deplore the crime and condemn the lynchers, but it will take more than resolutions of condemnation to wipe out the stain on the community. What industrious, respectable Negro will stay in such a community if he can get away? What industrious respectable white citizen will care to make his home where a mob can take any man, white or black, against whom its passions have been inflamed, and hang him in a quiet, orderly manner, without attempt to protect him either by the "best citizens" or the sworn officers of the law?

henry-golden-atlanta-1920-08-01.A1:
SUES TRACTION CO. WORLD CONVENTION FOR $20,000 OF NEGROES ON
Atlanta, Ga., Aug. 5.—Holding the Georgia Railway and Power Company responsible for, criminal acts of its employees, Mrs. Daisy Taylor, colored, filed suit for $20,000 damages against that corporation for the loss of her husband last Sunday night when he was killed by a conductor on the Inman Park line.

In the bill of complaint, filed by Attorney J. Walter LeCrew, the woman sets out that Henry Golden, the slain man, was her husband and that he was killed without provocation by W. R. Taylor, the conductor. She charges the company with negligence in employing the conductor.

Taylor is now under $2,000 bond waiting trial in Police Court August 5, when a number of Inman Park residents have been summoned to appear as witnesses.

john-barnes-new-york-1920-08-16.A1:
Two Shot, Riot Caused by Port Workers' Fight
Negro Strike Breakers Pursued by Longshoremen to the Elevated Trains; Passengers in Panic
Many Hurt in the Battle
Bullets, Bricks and Bottles Throw Residents of 14th Street Into Hysterics
In a battle between striking white longshoremen and negro strike breakers in Fourteenth Street, near Ninth Avenue, last evening, two of the strikers were shot and seriously wounded and many of the negroes received minor injuries.

A crowd of the negro strike breakers, pursued by white men armed with clubs, fled to the platform of the Fourteenth Street station of the Ninth Avenue Elevated and created a panic among two score-waiting passengers. Some of the negroes boarded a train and ran through the cars, yelling and waving their dock hooks. Many women in the coaches became hysterical.

About twenty-five of the negro longshoremen were walking toward the elevated station when a shower of bricks, stones and bottles fell about them. In another moment about thirty-five white men, all said to be striking port workers, were charging down on the negroes. Bricks were hurled from every direction and in hand-to-hand combats the whites are said to have used clubs and bottles.

Fighting Causes Panic

A running fight began. Hysterical women ran to the street to rescue children from the mob, and the breaking of door panels and windows by flying missiles caused consternation among residents and storekeepers.

A riot call was telephoned to the Charles Street station and the reserves boarded motor cars and rushed to the scene. By the time the police arrived, however, the bulk of both fighting factions had disappeared and only the wounded remained.

The white men who were shot are Daniel Curran, of 73 Gansevoort Street, wounded in the right chest, and James Kearns, of 129 East 123d Street, who received a gunshot wound in the right leg. Both were sent to St. Vincent's Hospital.

Police Find Injured

Among the injured negroes were John Barnes, of 251 West Sixty-first Street, who was lying unconscious on Ninth Avenue when the police arrived; Benjamin McNeal, of 161 West 140th Street, and Emil Howard, of 151 West 147th Street. Ambulance surgeons from St. Vincent's dressed the wounds of the negroes and sent them home. Their injuries were declared not serious.

The police say the identity of the persons who fired the shots has not been established. The firing is attributed to the strike breakers.

The negroes are employed on Piers 13 and 14, North River, of the Morgan Steamship line.

With Clubs.
SCORES BADLY BATTERED
One man is dying in a hospital, another was shot in the leg and scores suffered battered heads in a race riot in West Fourteenth street late yesterday afternoon between striking coastwise longshoremen and negro strikebreakers. The battle developed into a running fight that lasted more than half an hour, during which numerous shots were fired and stones were hurled through windows. It took the reserves of two precincts to restore order.

The negroes, apparently fearing the wrath of the strikers, who had demanded their discharge Saturday as one of the conditions for settling the strike, bolted from the police escort that had been conducting them to the Ninth avenue elevated station at Christopher street since the strike began in March, and darted into West Fourteenth street. One of the negroes, seeing the strikers closing in on him, pulled a pistol and fired into the air.

Almost instantly Fourteenth street was a battle ground. The negroes gashed into the strikers, pummelling them with their fists or with barrel staves they picked up in front of the commission merchants' stalls that line both sides of the street. Outnumbered by the strikers the negroes ran east to Ninth avenue, hurling stones at the strikers as they ran and tackling any white man that appeared in their path. At Ninth avenue they turned south to Hudson street and then ran to Thirteenth street, where they doubled back toward the river front.

By this time hurry calls for the reserves had been sent in to the Charles and West Twentieth street stations. The policemen arrived just as the negroes turned into West Thirteenth street, and they waded into the crowd swinging their nightsticks. The negroes were huddled into doorways in Ninth avenue while the strikers were being driven east in Thirteenth street toward Eighth avenue.

When order was restored the police discovered four men, two of them negroes, lying unconscious in Fourteenth street, between Ninth and Tenth avenues. Ambulances were summoned from New York Hospital and the four were hurried there. Daniel Curran, 18 years old, of 73 Gansevoort street, had been shot through the abdomen. Joseph Kearons, 25, a longshoreman, of 129 East 123d street, had been shot in the right leg. Daniel Johnson, 43, of 620 Lenox avenue, and Joseph Barnes, 49, of 251 West Sixty-first street, the negroes, suffered lacerations of the head.

The striking longshoremen will meet to-night at St. Veronica's Hall, Washington and Barrow streets, to receive a report from their leaders on the proposition they made to return to work provided their employers discharge the non-union men at work on the piers.
john-barnes-new-york-1920-08-16.A3:
Negroes, Whites, in Riots Over Strike
New York, Aug. 16.—Two men were shot and four others hurt by missiles thrown during a fight between striking longshoremen and negro non-union workmen at Ninth avenue and 14th street tonight. The trouble started when a crowd of non-union men, on their way from the piers, encountered a number of strikers, who, according to the police, started throwing rocks and bottles. Revolvers were drawn and a number of shots fired, two of which took effect among the strikers. Police reserves were summoned and the crowd dispersed before arrests could be made.

A meeting of strikers, scheduled tonight for the purpose of voting on the question of returning to work was not held. Union officials could not be reached to explain the reason.

New York, Aug. 20.---Monday night after a battle that lasted several hours between longshoremen, four members of the Race and two white men were injured and taken to St. Vincent's Hospital suffering from bullet wounds and lacerated scalp. Twenty-five men of color acting as strike breakers for the Morgan line pier near the foot of West 11th street striking longshoremen as they were returning home at 9th avenue and 11th street. russell-thomas-jones-station-1920-06-13.A1:
FLEES FROM HOME TO ESCAPE ASSAULT
Macon, Ga., Aug. 6.—Russell Thomas, a faithful old farmer, his two children and wife are in this city today penniless. It is not Thomas' fault. His only crime was that his face was not white, and he could not demand his rights before local courts. Thomas was driven from his farm because he refused to let his children slave for a plantation owner. Thomas rented from Mrs. Janie Etheridge (white) 38 acres of land and two mules at Jones Station, Ga., the land being rented for four bules of cotton per year and the mules for $30 each. Thomas had land under utilization (crop well). Thomas had the garden in good order with all vegetables growing. They possessed two cows and a calf, a hundred or more chickens and 13 head of hogs. On June 13 Grover Etheridge, Thomas, that he had purchased the property from his mother and that the tenants must do as he said. A few days later Etherdloe went to the Thomas cabin leading two mules. Mrs. Thomas and her daughter, Alberta, aged 14, and her son, Alvin, aged 8, were in the house. Thomas was given a quaint quip of the white man, for he ford the road he would be lynched. Etherdloe commanded the two children to "gelt hold of the mules," go to the field and plow until ordered to stop. They obeyed. Etherdloe was armed with a big stick and a pistol. Mrs. Thomas, knowing she had no protection, went bitterly as the little tots braced their mother, but a blow across the back from the white man's heavy club uninjured him. As night came the mother gathered her tired children about her, and over a long and dusty road the three truveled on foot until they reached this city, leaving behind them all they possessed, and have not been allowed to return. They are now residing in this city, at 151 Franklin street, in a desolate neighborhood of clothes and barely any household goods. To them Young, 247 Beckwith street, Atlanta, Ga., is endeavoring to regain the lost possession of the family. scott-garner-anderson-1920-07.A1:
PROBABLE LYNCHING AVERTED.
Negro Attacked Anderson Woman
—Officers Spirited Him Away.
Anderson, July 28. — Anderson is quiet this morning after the excitement of last night, when Scott Garner, a 14-year-old colored youth, is alleged to have attacked a prominent young white woman. Following arrest of the boy, he was identified by the woman, and local officers, by a clever ruse, fooled the crowd of people who had gathered, and as the mob chased a decoy automobile loaded with policemen, Deputy Sheriff Hilliard made his escape with the prisoner.

The young woman was attacked while standing in front of her home waiting the return of her husband, who had gone to put his automobile in the garage. The woman was unable to defend herself when seized by the negro, owing to the fact that she had her baby in her arms. The negro became frightened and ran when the young woman screamed and brought the husband to her assistance. The negro was later arrested at his home and taken before the woman, who, with his husband, identified him as the right person. News soon spread over the city of the affair, and within a short time a crowd had gathered which in all probability would have dealt severely with the negro had not the officers spirited him away.
